title: Reading Practice 11 - The Silk Road Trade Routes
description: IELTS Academic Reading practice about ancient trade networks connecting East and West.

stimuli.title: Passage 1: The Silk Road Trade Routes
stimuli.content:
A The Silk Road was not a single road but a vast network of overland and maritime trade routes that connected China with the Mediterranean world for nearly two millennia. The name was coined by German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877, though silk was just one of many commodities traded along these routes. The Silk Road facilitated the exchange not only of goods but also of ideas, religions, technologies, and diseases between civilisations that might otherwise have remained isolated from each other.

B The overland routes of the Silk Road stretched approximately 6,400 kilometres from Chang'an (modern Xi'an) in China through Central Asia to the eastern shores of the Mediterranean. The journey was extraordinarily dangerous, crossing some of the world's most inhospitable terrain including the Taklamakan Desert, the Pamir Mountains, and the steppes of Central Asia. Few merchants travelled the entire route; instead, goods typically passed through a chain of intermediaries, with each trader covering a portion of the journey.

C Beyond trade in physical goods, the Silk Road served as a conduit for cultural and intellectual exchange. Buddhism spread from India to China and East Asia along these routes, while Islam later spread in the opposite direction. Chinese inventions such as paper, printing, gunpowder, and the compass travelled westward along the Silk Road, profoundly affecting European civilisation. In return, Western innovations in glassmaking, metalworking, and agriculture reached East Asia.

D The decline of the overland Silk Road began in the 15th century as maritime trade routes became increasingly efficient. Portuguese explorers established sea routes to Asia that bypassed the Central Asian middlemen who had controlled the overland trade. However, China's Belt and Road Initiative has been described as a modern Silk Road, seeking to recreate ancient patterns of Eurasian connectivity through massive infrastructure investment.
